zh.title: 漢莎航空擬於九天內在空中巴士A320neo推出Starlink機上網路
zh.summary: 漢莎航空將於A320neo導入Starlink；預估2029年涵蓋集團全機隊
body: 漢莎航空（Lufthansa）即將在空中巴士（Airbus）A320neo 客機上推出高速 Starlink 機上網路服務，預計於 9 天內正式啟用。該架客機為該航空集團規畫安裝衛星網路設備的首架飛機，未來相關升級計畫預計將涵蓋旗下總計 850 架客機。
根據 Simple Flying 報導，機上網路升級計畫將逐步推廣至漢莎航空集團的營運體系中。漢莎航空集團目標於 2029 年前，完成旗下所有航空公司的 Starlink 機上網路配備與裝設。

en.title: Lufthansa to Launch Starlink WiFi on Airbus A320neo Within Nine Days
en.summary: Lufthansa will launch Starlink WiFi on Airbus A320neo aircraft, targeting group-wide coverage by 2029.
body: Lufthansa is set to launch high-speed Starlink inflight WiFi services on an Airbus A320neo aircraft within nine days. This initial aircraft deployment represents the very first step in a broader fleet connectivity initiative, which is planned to eventually cover a total of 850 jets across the airline group.

According to industry reporting by Simple Flying, the installation project will roll out progressively across all passenger flight operations. The Lufthansa Group targets full deployment across all of its group airlines with Starlink WiFi by 2029, bringing upgraded satellite internet connectivity to its fleet.

zh.title: 美空軍機器人製造C17鼻翼 首次重返天空
zh.summary: 美空軍用機器人製造C17鼻翼 讓受損戰機成功重返天空
body: 2025年3月4日凌晨，德克薩斯州達拉斯-福沃思地區遭遇強烈雷暴，龍捲風警告同時發布。位於Perot Field Fort Worth Alliance Airport的美國空軍第445後勤聯隊C-17 Globemaster III過夜停機時，風微爆風速接近每小時80英里，吹走兩架私人擁有的Bombardier Challenger商務噴射機，它們被吹向較大的軍用運輸機，碰撞左側機身，損壞機艙門、機身前部與鼻翼。
儘管機體仍具飛行能力，但無法立即執行任務。維修人員先進行臨時修護，讓飛機在起落架全程鎖定的狀態下飛返俄亥俄州萊特-帕特森空軍基地。基地維修隊修復了受損門與機身，但鼻翼更換成為最大難題。
波音公司評估後認為，沒有供應商願意為此單件鼻翼製造專用工具，因商業效益不足。修復嘗試也失敗，若等待供應方案可能需要兩年以上，對第445後勤聯隊而言不可接受。
因此，第445維修組轉向空軍快速持續辦公室（RSO）所屬的自動化與機器人團隊。該團隊認為受損鼻翼適合作為增量板成形（ISF）技術的驗證平台，該技術由機器人逐步壓塑金屬板，無需專用模具，適合低產量或唯一零件的快速製造。
2026年1月，在代頓大學研究院協助下，RSO開始製造替換鼻翼。經過機械成形後，零件接受結構測試與反覆試裝，最終於四月通過最終適合評估獲得安裝批准。
零件安裝完成後，C-17重新起飛。這標誌著首次使用空軍ISF技術製造的元件在實役飛機上飛行，也為老舊軍機隊伍提供了一種當原備件停產時的潛在解決方案。

en.title: US Air Force Uses Robotic Manufacturing to Replace C-17 Nose Panel, Jet Returns to Flight
en.summary: US Air Force flies repaired C-17 after robotic nose-panel manufacture
body: In the early hours of 4 March 2025, severe thunderstorms swept across the Dallas‑Fort Worth area, spawning large hail, violent wind gusts and tornado warnings. At Perot Field Fort Worth Alliance Airport (AFW), a US Air Force C-17 Globemaster III from the 445th Airlift Wing was parked overnight when wind microbursts approaching 80 mph swept the airfield. Two privately owned Bombardier Challenger business jets broke free and were blown into the much larger military transport, smashing into the left side of the aircraft and damaging its access door, fuselage and nose section.

Although the jet remained flyable, it was not mission‑ready. A temporary repair allowed the aircraft to fly back to Wright‑Patterson AFB in Ohio with its landing gear locked down for the entire flight. Once home, maintenance crews repaired the door and fuselage, but the nose panel proved a far greater challenge.

Boeing determined that no supplier was willing to manufacture the single replacement panel because producing the specialised tooling for one isolated component made no commercial sense. A repair attempt also failed, leaving the prospect of a year‑plus wait for a solution followed by another year of work—an outcome the 445th Airlift Wing deemed unacceptable.

Instead of accepting a prolonged grounding, the 445th Maintenance Group turned to the Air Force Rapid Sustainment Office (RSO) and its Automation and Robotics team. They proposed using Incremental Sheet Forming (ISF), a robotic metal‑forming process that gradually reshapes a flat sheet without dedicated tooling, making it ideal for unique or extremely low‑volume parts.

Working with engineers from the University of Dayton Research Institute, the RSO began manufacturing the replacement panel in January 2026. The panel proceeded from robotic forming to structural testing and repeated fit checks, receiving approval for installation after a final fit assessment in April.

The panel was installed and the C‑17 returned to flight. This marks the first time a component produced using the Air Force’s ISF technology has flown on an operational aircraft, offering a potential solution to the sustainment problem faced by ageing military fleets when original parts are no longer available.
